hints: Hint 1: Think about what makes a radian special compared to degrees - focus on the two lengths that define an angle at the centre of a circle.
parts.proper_answer: The radian is the angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc of length equal to the radius of the circle.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture the angle at the centre**
Imagine you are at the centre of a circle. An angle opens out and cuts off a short curved piece of the circumference. That curved piece is called the arc length, call it $s$, and the circle has radius $r$.

Step 2: **State the special condition**
One radian is the specific case when those two lengths match exactly. In symbols, $$\theta = \frac{s}{r}$$ and $\theta = 1 \text{ rad}$ when $s = r$.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem:
A circular metal disc spins horizontally about a vertical axis, as shown in Fig. 1.1.

{{figure:figure_1_1}}

Fig. 1.1 (not to scale)

A piece of modelling clay is attached to the disc.

For the instant when the piece of modelling clay is in the position shown, draw on Fig. 1.1:
parts.text: an arrow, labelled $V$, showing the direction of the velocity of the modelling clay

markscheme_points.text: arrow, labelled V, pointing in NE direction

hints: Hint 1: Look at the rotation arrow at the top of the disc and imagine which way the clay must be moving at its south-east position if it follows that rotation.
parts.proper_answer: Arrow labelled V drawn from the clay tangentially to its circular path, pointing approximately north-east, perpendicular to the radius.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Velocity is always along the tangent**
Even though the clay moves in a circle, at any instant its velocity points straight along the tangent to the circle at that point. It never points outwards or inwards.

Step 2: **Use the sense of rotation**
The top of the disc moves to the left, so the rotation is anticlockwise as seen from above. At the south-east position of the clay, the tangent for anticlockwise motion points up and to the right, roughly north-east. Draw a short arrow from the clay in that direction and label it $V$.

markscheme_points.text: arrow, labelled A, pointing in NW direction

hints: Hint 1: Remember that circular motion needs a continuous change in velocity direction - think about which direction the pull must act to keep the clay on its circle.
parts.proper_answer: Arrow labelled A drawn from the clay pointing directly toward the centre of the disc, approximately north-west.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Acceleration points to the centre**
In uniform circular motion the speed stays the same but the direction of velocity keeps changing. That change requires a centripetal acceleration that always points toward the centre of the circle.

Step 2: **Draw it from the clay position**
Join the clay to the centre dot with a straight line in your mind. Your arrow $A$ must lie along that line, starting at the clay and pointing inward, which is roughly north-west for the position shown.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.part_stem:
The metal disc in Fig. 1.1 has a radius of $9.3\text{ cm}$.
The centre of gravity of the modelling clay is $1.2\text{ cm}$ from the rim of the disc and moves with a speed of $0.68\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
parts.text: Calculate the angular speed $\omega$ of the disc.
hints: Hint 1: Start by finding the actual radius of the clay's circle - it is not the full 9.3 cm because the centre of gravity is 1.2 cm in from the rim.
Hint 2: Recall how linear speed $v$ and angular speed $\omega$ are linked through the radius, then rearrange to find $\omega$ and convert cm to m.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the true radius of motion**
The disc radius is $9.3 \text{ cm}$ but the clay centre is $1.2 \text{ cm}$ from the rim, so it moves on a smaller circle: $$r = 9.3 \text{ cm} - 1.2 \text{ cm} = 8.1 \text{ cm} = 0.081 \text{ m}$$ Always convert to metres before using $v$ in $\text{m s}^{-1}$.

Step 2: **Link linear and angular speed**
For any point on a rotating body: $$v = r\omega$$ Rearranged: $$\omega = \frac{v}{r} = \frac{0.68}{0.081}$$ This gives $$\omega = 8.4 \text{ rad s}^{-1}$$ to 2 s.f.

marking_points.text: $v = r\omega$

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: Calculate the acceleration $a$ of the centre of gravity of the modelling clay.
hints: Hint 1: Think about which formula connects the acceleration toward the centre to the speed and radius you already know.
Hint 2: Decide whether to use $v$ and $r$ directly or to use your $\omega$ value from (c)(i), then check the unit for acceleration.
parts.proper_answer: $a = v^2/r = 0.68^2/0.081 = 5.7 \text{ m s}^{-2}$ toward the centre.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Choose the centripetal formula**
The magnitude of the inward acceleration is given by: $$a = \frac{v^2}{r}$$ which is identical to $$a = r\omega^2$$ Use whichever data is most direct. Here $v$ and $r$ are known.

Step 2: **Substitute and calculate**
$$a = \frac{(0.68)^2}{0.081}$$ $$a = 5.7 \text{ m s}^{-2}$$ The direction is toward the centre of the disc. This is quite large compared to everyday accelerations because $v$ is squared.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text:
A second piece of modelling clay is attached to the disc in the position shown in Fig. 1.2.

{{figure:figure_1_2}}

Fig. 1.2

The second piece of modelling clay has a larger mass than the first piece.

By placing one tick ($\checkmark$) in each row, complete Table 1.1 to show how the quantities indicated compare for the two pieces of modelling clay.

Table 1.1

quantity | less for second piece than first piece | same for both pieces | greater for second piece than first piece
angular speed |  |  | 
linear speed |  |  | 
acceleration |  |  |

markscheme_points.text: angular speed: same for both pieces
linear speed: less for second piece than first piece
acceleration: less for second piece than first piece

hints: Hint 1: Think about the disc as a rigid body - do all points complete one rotation in the same time regardless of how far out they are?
Hint 2: Now use $v = r\omega$ to compare linear speeds when $\omega$ is fixed but $r$ is smaller for the second piece near the centre.
Hint 3: Extend the same radius argument to acceleration using $a = r\omega^2$, and ignore the mass information which does not affect these kinematic quantities.
parts.proper_answer: angular speed: same for both pieces. linear speed: less for second piece than first piece. acceleration: less for second piece than first piece.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Angular speed is shared**
The disc is rigid, so every point turns through the same angle in the same time. That means $\omega$ is the same for both pieces. Mass has no effect on $\omega$. Tick same for both pieces.

Step 2: **Linear speed follows radius**
With $$v = r\omega$$ and $\omega$ fixed, $v$ is directly proportional to $r$. The second piece is much closer to the axis, so its $r$ is smaller and its $v$ is smaller. Tick less for second piece than first piece.

Step 3: **Acceleration follows radius**
With $$a = r\omega^2$$ and $\omega$ fixed, $a$ is also directly proportional to $r$. The smaller $r$ of the second piece gives a smaller centripetal acceleration. Tick less for second piece than first piece. The larger mass would need a larger centripetal force ($F = ma$) but does not change $\omega$, $v$ or $a$.
